From sheet attached to box:
Also includes recordings made for Decca, Deutsche Grammophon and EMI.
This limited-edition box set brings together for the very first time one of the most extensive discographies of any pianist. Alfred Brendel’s place among the greatest musicians of the 20th and 21st centuries is assured. Renowned for his masterly interpretations of the works of Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms, Schumaan and Liszt, he is one of the indisputable authorities in musical life today.

This 114-CD box includes:
Part 1 Mozart, Bach and Haydn
Part 2 Beethoven
Part 3 The Romantics
Part 4 Chamber, Lieder and Live recordings
Plus A 220-page illustrated book with a new appreciation by Mischa Donat, indices of works by composer and recording date, new and archive photographs and Alfred Brendel’s personal recollections on his career.

This compilation ℗ 2015 Decca Music Group Limited
© 2015 Decca Music Group Limited

The packaging features an outer box, with four smaller boxes inside which serve to both subdivide and house the CD card sleeves into the above mentioned 4 Parts.
In the booklet, the foreword, new appreciation and personal recollections are in English, French and German.

This first release can be be distinguished from later reissues by use of an umbrella icon (AJB) on lower left of box top and in the booklet.

Total Playing Time: 71:09

Dvořák's Symphony No. 7 was recorded on July 17 and 18, 1963, on both three-track 35mm film and half-inch three-track tape.  Because of the present unavailability of the film, this CD has been mastered from the original three-track tape, as was the original LP, SR 90516.  The Symphony No. 8 was recorded on June 19 and 20, 1959, on half-inch three-track tape and was originally released as SR90236.  Both Symphonies were recorded in Watford Town Hall, outside London, using three Telefunken 201 microphones.

Only ORIGINAL MASTERS used for transfer to Compact Disc.

This is the 1985 version mastered by John Dent.

Originally packaged in smooth edged jewel case with a black tray. 8-page booklet with lyrics and credits.

Page 6 of the booklet has credit: Mastered by - John Dent at The Sound Clinic, London. This version does not credit Sting as a co-writer for Money for Nothing. See images.

[r=2825382], also released in 1985, was mastered by Bob Ludwig.
Additionally, the entire [l486734] series of CD albums reissued in 1996 were all remastered by Bob Ludwig.

John Dent mastering is authentically known on discs with 02, 03 and 06 last digits on matrix.
Matrices ending with 07 and higher - Bob Ludwig mastering.

The John Dent mastering is reported to be reversed, compared to Ludwig's mastering.
Start of track 1, listen for gentle cymbal (high-hat) hits in right channel and no cymbal in left channel.
Reported correct and intended position of this hit-hat cymbal is to the left channel.

Ⓟ 2000, 2001, 2003, 2004, 2008 & 2010 Alpha Productions / Ⓒ 2011 Alpha Productions / outhere (www.alpha-prod.com).

CD1 recorded August 2000 & August 2001 at Paris, Chapelle de l'hôpital Notre-Dame de Bon Secours.
CD2 recorded at l'Arsenal de Metz in June 2003.
CD3 recorded in February and August 2004 at l'Arsenal de Metz.
CD4 recorded at Temple Saint-Jean de Mulhouse in July 2008 & at l'Arsenal de Metz in February 2004 (BWV 1061).
CD5 recorded February 2004 at l'Arsenal de Metz & March 2010 and May 2010 at Temple Saint-Jean de Mulhouse.
CD6 recorded February 2004 at l'Arsenal de Metz (BWV 1065) & March 2010 and May 2010 at Temple Saint-Jean de Mulhouse.

Total duration: 6h28.

The glossy 160-page booklet contains notes in French, English and German.
As well as lots of photographs, track-lists and credits-lists.
Each CD is stored in a cardboard sleeve with the original artwork as per CD release.
The booklet and 6 CD's are stored in a luxurious reinforced fully laminated cardboard box.

disques.notes_discogs:
1-32: recorded in 1955 (when Gould was 23)
Extracted from Liner Notes by James Murray about this recording:
 "Following rave reviews at his New York and Washington débuts in early 1955, Gould was offered a contract by CBS when this recording of the Goldberg Variations are made. At these sessions he approached the variations first, completing most of the recording relatively quickly. His approach to the opening "unassuming Sarabande" on which the variations are based gave the engineers a headache as his perfectionism took hold: the version chosen was in fact the 21st take!".

33-47: recorded in 1978
Remastered for Alto 

Total Time: 79:38

disques.notes_discogs:
Total Playing Time: 172:35

Sylvia was recorded on June 28 and 29, 1958, in Watford Town Hall, outside London.  Recording sessions for Coppélia took place in Northrop Auditorium in Minneapolis on December 21 and 22, 1957.  Both works were recorded on 3-track half-inch tape using one 201 and two M-56 Telefunken microphones.  Sylvia was originally released as SR2-9006 and Coppélia as SR2-9005.

Only ORIGINAL MASTERS used for transfer to Compact Disc.

disques.notes_discogs:
Recorded on April 20, 1953 at WOR Studios, New York City
Tracks 1 and 3 are CD bonus tracks

The note printed at the bottom side of the back cover reads: 

"Miles Davis' first and third Blue Note sessions are presented in complete recorded order on Miles Davis Volume One ([url=https://www.discogs.com/Miles-Davis-Volume-1/release/1242569]B2-81501[/url]). Like that compact disc, this one also does not conform to the album's vinyl counterpart. This one offers Davis' second session complete and in recording order with two previously unissued alternate takes. The original tapes on all but the previously unissued selections are lost and we have spent considerable time improving and repairing the sound of the tapes with which we were left."
